We propose to compare the effect of a newly approved product to control pyrexia and BRD in cattle that
is a combination of tulathromycin and ketoprofen with a product with similar claims that is a combination
of florfenicol and flunixin meglumine. We plan to measure rectal temperature, prostaglandin synthesis,
serum amyloid A concentrations, eye temperature, activity and drug concentrations over a series of
timepoints to quantify and compare the duration of effect for these two products in cattle.
(Please provide a concise narrative review of the literature and basis for the study):
When the bovine immune system encounters a pathogen, inflammatory mediators initiate systemic
changes known as the sickness response which includes pyrexia. Cattle often manifest the sickness
response as a result of bovine respiratory disease which is treated with an antibiotic, and may be more
attenuated with the addition of an NSAID as well (Toaff-Rosenstein, 2015). It has been established that
the co-formulation of ketoprofen with tulathromycin alters the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic
profile of ketoprofen in cattle, resulting in pyrexia being controlled for a longer period of time than with
ketoprofen alone (Koster, 2021). Both tulathromycin + ketoprofen and florfenicol + flunixin meglumine
have been shown to reduce rectal temperature 6 h post-trt compared to tulathromycin or florfenicol
alone (FDA, 2021; Thiry, 2014). However, due to tulathromycin + ketoprofen recently being approved for
use in cattle, a comparison of the two combinations of an antimicrobial + NSAID have not been
evaluated to determine if one controls pyrexia or inflammatory biomarkers for a longer period than the

12 intact, yearling, male, Holstein calves will be enrolled onto the crossover study. Calves are currently
housed at LAHA under IACUC protocol #3904. They will remain at LAHA for the duration of the proposed
study. Calves will be inoculated with LPS by subcutaneous injection at a dose of 5 µg/kg at the 0 h
timepoint (De Koster, 2021). All 12 calves will first be their own controls with rectal temperatures, IRT
images, and blood samples taken via jugular venipuncture to quantify PGE metabolite, serum amyloid A
and drug concentrations at 10 study timepoints. Accelerometers will also be placed on their left rear leg
for the study duration. Blood will be collected from the jugular vein by venipuncuture using a syringe or
vacutainer and a 16 G 1.5 inch needle. The ten study collection timepoints are 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24,
A 3 week washout period will then occur which has been established as an appropriate endotoxin washout
Calves will again be inoculated with LPS by subcutaneous injection at a dose of 5 µg/kg at the 0 h
timepoint (De Koster, 2021). Then 6 of the calves will be administered tulathromycin + ketoprofen at the
labeled SQ dosage in the neck of 2.5 mg tulathromycin and 3 mg ketoprofen/kg (1.1 mL/100 lb)
bodyweight and 6 of the calves will be administered florfenicol + flunixin meglumine at the labeled SQ
dosage of 6 mL/100 pounds of bodyweight. Then the study collection timepoints will be repeated at 0, 1,
2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h following inoculation with the same biosamples taken as mentioned

90.10 Justification of Animal Numbers / Data: Analysis:
Research, testing, and teaching activities should be designed to provide a statistically significant result
with a minimum number of animals. The specific method by which the number of animals was
determined must be clearly stated. Statistical techniques and/or power analysis are appropriate in most
cases to maximize the usefulness of the data generated from each animal. However, the IACUC
acknowledges that the basis for an appropriate justification of animal numbers depends largely on the
nature of the study itself. Prior experience and expertise with the model in question may be taken into
account as well, but must be carefully documented in the protocol. The cost of the animal should not be
considered as the primary justification for the use of a particular species or model. Consultation with a
biostatistician or use of statistical software during the design phase of the experiment may be useful.
This website may be helpful in performing a power analysis: http://statpages.org

Replacement refers to the "equipment, technologies, approaches, and/or procedures that directly
replace or avoid the use of animals in experiments by incorporating non-animal methods where they
would otherwise have been used." Replacement can be full/absolute replacement avoiding any and all
use of animals, or partial/relative replacement where animals are still used to provide tissue, cells,
and/or organs but experiments are conducted in vitro. Replacement can also include the use of animals
that have been slaughtered for meat or euthanized due to other purposes.

In order to evaluate potential for pain and/or distress, the KSU IACUC requires an approved plan of how
pain or distress will be minimized and documentation of how observations of animals will be recorded. All
procedures performed upon an animal should be listed on an Animal Monitoring Plan (AMP) form.
The AMP form along with the Animal Observation Record (AOR) detail how you will observe your
animals and what actions you will take in order to minimize pain or distress associated with your
research project. Examples of procedures needing an AMP include surgical procedure, animals that
undergo anesthesia, animals experimentally infected with an infectious disease, experimental
vaccination, or animals inoculated with potential tumor forming cells. Exceptions to the use of the AMP
and AOR would be simple procedures with minimal physiological effect upon the animal, examples of
which include blood collection, or injection of therapeutic drugs.
If an AMP is included in your approved IACUC document, it is your responsibility as the PI to
assure that the AMP activities will be used as described in the approved protocol. It it is your
responsibility to be able to provide documentation for the activities called for in the AMP.

(Experimental studies may involve procedures that cause clinical symptoms or morbidity in animals.
The IACUC must consider the selection of the most appropriate endpoint(s). This requires careful
consideration of the scientific requirements of the study, expected and possible adverse effects
research animals may experience (pain, distress, illness, etc.), the most likely time course and
progression of those adverse effects, and the earliest most predictive indicators of present or
impending adverse effects. Optimally, studies are terminated when animals begin to exhibit clinical
signs of disease if this endpoint is compatible with meeting the research objectives. Such endpoints are
preferable to death or moribundity as endpoints since they minimize pain and distress. The use of
death of the animal as an endpoint is strongly discouraged and must be justified to the IACUC -
